title: Abstract Factory: create products that agree

opening.title: Two individually valid objects can be a bad pair
keyPoints: A sender writes one digit
A receiver reads that representation
The decoded value must equal the original
opening.narration: A sender and receiver can each look correct on their own and still fail together. Our teaching protocol has ten possible values, zero through nine. One family writes a bare digit such as 7. Another writes a framed digit such as [7]. The receiving object must understand the same family that the sending object used. We are not sending a real network message; the wire in this chapter is a string passed between functions. That small model lets us inspect every accepted value. The key problem is agreement between two products. It will lead us to select a whole family instead of making two unrelated choices.
actions: Ask learners to decode 7 and [7] under each proposed rule.
Write the round-trip promise in words before introducing factory names.
opening.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → A writer and reader must agree

question.prompt: What is the central promise connecting encoder and decoder?
question.answer: For every allowed digit, reading the string produced by the matching encoder must return the original value.

opening.title: Treat compatibility as an explicit requirement
keyPoints: Numbers outside 0–9 are rejected
Shape and digit content are both checked
Cross-family input must not silently pass
opening.narration: An encoder turns a value into a representation. A decoder turns that representation back into a value. Those names tell us their jobs but do not prove they agree. Our requirements include positive cases and rejection cases: all ten digits must round-trip, an out-of-range integer must fail, and malformed text must fail. Framing also has two parts. The brackets must be right, and the middle character must be a decimal digit. A string like [x] has the right shape and the wrong content. Writing these checks before choosing the design helps us catch a family assembled from the wrong members later.
actions: Build a small accepted/rejected table for 0, 9, 10, [7], and [x].
Ask which tests are about numeric range and which are about representation.
opening.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → The failure is a mismatched pair

question.prompt: Why is accepting [x] a defect even though its brackets are correct?
question.answer: The frame is structurally valid, but the contained character is outside the digit protocol. Both conditions are required.

opening.title: A single protocol starts with two functions
keyPoints: No factory is needed for one fixed pair
A colon introduces each value from the list
Subtracting character 0 gives the checked digit value
opening.narration: The simplest version uses two ordinary functions. The loop's colon means take each value from the list on the right and run the body with that value. Each iteration writes a digit, then reads it back. std::to_string produces text; it does not change the integer into a character by casting. In the reader, we first require exactly one decimal digit. Only then do we subtract the character '0'. Decimal digit characters are consecutive in C++, so this gives the numeric value after the range check. The three printed lines demonstrate normal behavior for the chosen inputs. They do not replace the exhaustive ten-value check in the chapter program.
actions: Predict the three output lines, then run.
Point to the colon and describe one complete loop iteration.
opening.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch02.json → A writer and reader must agree

question.prompt: Why does read_digit subtract the character 0 rather than the integer zero?
question.answer: The input is an encoded character. Subtracting the code for character 0 converts a validated decimal character to its numeric value.

opening.title: A mismatch can compile and still fail at the boundary
keyPoints: Framed output is a valid string
Plain input requires exactly one digit
Type agreement does not imply protocol agreement
opening.narration: This sender produces [4], and the receiver expects exactly one character. There is no C++ type error: the sender returns std::string and the reader accepts a string reference. Execution rejects the three-character input. The final control call shows the reader can handle its own valid input, so blaming all decoding would be too broad. The defect is the pair selected during setup. This same problem occurs when a serializer and parser disagree about a version or when a user-interface family mixes incompatible parts. Abstract Factory will move family selection into one object. It reduces opportunities for mismatches, but we will still need behavioral tests.
actions: Predict whether the error is at build time or run time.
Run and use the final control line to narrow the diagnosis.
opening.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch02.json → The failure is a mismatched pair

question.prompt: Why can the compiler accept this mismatched pair?
question.answer: Both sides use compatible C++ types. Their different interpretation of the string is a runtime protocol rule, not encoded in those types.

code.expectedStdout:
sent=[4]
receiver rejected the family

mechanism.title: Choose the family once, then ask for its members
keyPoints: CodecFactory offers encoder and decoder
Each concrete factory supplies one matching family
The client depends on product roles
mechanism.narration: A family is a set of objects intended to work together. CodecFactory declares two creation operations because the client needs two product roles: an encoder and a decoder. PlainFactory supplies the plain members, while FramedFactory supplies the framed members. round_trip receives one factory and asks that same factory for both products. It does not select an encoder from one source and a decoder from an unrelated source. This is the organizing idea of Abstract Factory. The client still knows what sending and receiving mean. It simply stops naming the concrete format classes. New family choices can then be made at setup without scattering those names through the protocol workflow.
actions: Trace both creation calls from the single factory parameter.
Ask which concrete product names disappear from the client.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → The failure is a mismatched pair

question.prompt: Which object should round_trip use to obtain both products?
question.answer: The same selected CodecFactory object, so one family decision controls both creation requests.

theory.what: One interface creates several related product roles.
theory.why: Independent setup choices can mix incompatible protocol members.
theory.invariant: A factory supplies products that satisfy one round-trip contract together.
theory.risk: A faulty override can still return a member from the wrong family.

mechanism.title: Separate product roles keep the interface honest
keyPoints: Encoder writes; Decoder reads
Neither product is a subtype of the other
Compatibility is a relationship between behaviors
mechanism.narration: A decoder is not a special kind of encoder. Giving them a common do_everything interface would hide their different duties. In the chapter, each role has its own base class and virtual operation. The plain and framed encoders share Encoder; the plain and framed decoders share Decoder. Factories create across these two hierarchies. This distinction helps us read the UML: inheritance arrows stay within a role, while creation dependencies connect a factory to its concrete products. The compatibility rule sits across the pair: read after write returns the original allowed value. That rule is not an inheritance arrow and is not proved by making the products share a base class.
actions: Name the operation on each product interface.
Explain why the pair contract belongs in tests as well as documentation.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → Two product roles are not one inheritance tree

question.prompt: Would inheriting Decoder from Encoder enforce a matching protocol?
question.answer: No. It confuses distinct roles and says nothing about whether read and write agree on their representations.

mechanism.title: A borrowed factory can create owned products
keyPoints: const CodecFactory& borrows configuration choice
Local unique_ptr values own the products
This implementation stores no back-pointer to the factory
mechanism.narration: The reference parameter lets round_trip use a factory that remains owned by its caller. const stops the client from calling non-const factory operations through that parameter. The products are different: each returned unique_ptr gives round_trip responsibility for one object's cleanup. If the second creation throws, the first local owner is still destroyed as the function exits through the exception. The concrete products here do not refer back to their factory, so their behavior does not require keeping the factory alive. That conclusion follows from this source code, not from the pattern name. A future factory that lends shared configuration to products would need an explicit lifetime rule.
actions: Mark the borrowed parameter and the two owning local variables.
Ask how storing a factory reference inside a product would change the contract.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → Two product roles are not one inheritance tree

question.prompt: If decoder creation throws after encoder creation succeeded, who releases the encoder?
question.answer: The encoder local unique_ptr releases it during exception cleanup. The borrowed factory remains the caller’s responsibility.

mechanism.title: Guard the shape before reading its parts
keyPoints: Check wire size first
Only then inspect brackets and the middle digit
Shape validation and value validation are separate
mechanism.narration: The framed reader checks for length three before calling front or back. The logical-or operator, written as two vertical bars, stops when one condition is already true. If the size is wrong, the later bracket checks do not run. This matters because front and back require a nonempty string. Once the three-character shape and brackets are confirmed, the reader extracts the middle character and reuses the plain digit reader. That is a local parsing dependency, not evidence that the framed decoder belongs to the plain factory family. A parser must reject both missing structure and invalid content. Testing only [7] would miss [x], an empty string, or extra trailing text.
actions: Trace the guard for an empty string and then for [x].
Ask which layer rejects each input and why.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → Parsing is part of the contract

question.prompt: Why must the size check appear before front and back in this guard?
question.answer: Short-circuit evaluation skips those operations for an invalid length, including empty input where front and back would be unsafe.

mechanism.title: The factory promises compatibility; tests check it
keyPoints: Override checks signatures
Return types do not encode the family pairing
Exhaust all ten valid values and test malformed input
mechanism.narration: Suppose FramedFactory accidentally returns PlainDecoder from decoder. That return can satisfy unique_ptr<Decoder>, and the override can compile perfectly. The family contract is still broken. This is why the chapter's round_trip checks the decoded result, and why main exercises all ten valid values. A successful round-trip for one value may miss a reader that mishandles another digit. Rejection tests add different evidence: inputs from the wrong family and malformed strings must fail as promised. In a larger protocol, complete enumeration may be impossible, so boundary tests and generated cases matter. The pattern organizes responsibility; it does not turn behavioral promises into automatic mathematical proof.
actions: Propose the faulty factory change verbally and classify whether it compiles.
Ask why all valid digits still matter after one mismatch test.
mechanism.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → A factory encourages compatibility; it does not prove it

question.prompt: What test exposes a framed factory that returns a plain decoder?
question.answer: Request both products from that factory and round-trip a valid digit such as 7. The plain decoder rejects the framed string.

closing.title: Expect cheap new families and expensive new roles
keyPoints: Adding a family implements existing creation operations
Adding a product role changes every factory
Choose the design for the likely change
closing.narration: Every abstraction favors some changes over others. Adding TaggedFactory is local because encoder and decoder are already the agreed roles. The new family supplies those two products while round_trip continues using the same interface. Adding a third role, such as a validator product, is a wider change if it becomes a required operation on CodecFactory. Every concrete factory must then decide what to return. This is a practical maintenance cost, not a flaw we can wish away. Before choosing Abstract Factory, ask whether you expect many new families of stable roles or frequent changes to the list of roles itself. A small bundle-returning function may be easier when the family set is fixed.
actions: Have students list the files affected by each proposed change.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → A factory encourages compatibility; it does not prove it

question.prompt: Which change is more local: adding TaggedFactory or adding a required checksum product to CodecFactory?
question.answer: Adding TaggedFactory is more local. A required new product role changes the base factory contract and every concrete factory.

comparisons.label: New family
comparisons.text: Implement the existing Encoder, Decoder, and CodecFactory roles.

comparisons.label: New product role
comparisons.text: Revise the shared factory interface and all family implementations.

closing.title: Do not split a good codec merely to fit a diagram
keyPoints: One cohesive codec may be enough
A returned bundle can keep setup together
Compile-time families can provide stronger constraints
closing.narration: A design pattern should solve a real separation problem. If one object naturally owns both writing and reading, keeping a single codec may express the requirement more clearly. If separate objects are useful but no runtime family switching is needed, a function can return a struct containing a matched pair. When the family is known during compilation, distinct family types or templates can rule out some mismatches earlier. Abstract Factory is valuable here because separate send and receive products are required and clients select a family through a stable runtime interface. Choose deliberately. More interfaces do not automatically mean more safety; they can also create more places for a configuration mistake.
actions: Ask learners to defend one-object and two-object designs under different lifetimes.
Distinguish runtime flexibility from compile-time constraints.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → A factory encourages compatibility; it does not prove it

question.prompt: What requirement would support keeping one Codec object instead of two product interfaces?
question.answer: If sending and receiving are always used together with one shared lifetime and no need for separate components, one cohesive codec can be simpler.

closing.title: Recall the contract, then reconstruct the architecture
keyPoints: One family selection supplies both roles
read(write(value)) equals value
Malformed and mixed-family representations are rejected
closing.narration: Try rebuilding the idea from the failure rather than from a class diagram. Independently chosen senders and receivers can disagree about string format. We therefore choose one family object and request both roles from it. The client owns the returned products and checks the same round-trip promise through their interfaces. Now imagine supporting a new tagged format d=7. Describe the new encoder, decoder, and factory, then list the old tests that must continue to pass. Finally, explain what the pattern cannot guarantee: a badly written factory can still return the wrong member, and the compiler may accept it. This final boundary is part of understanding the pattern, not a reason to skip it.
actions: Close the diagrams and ask students to reconstruct the three roles for a tagged family.
End by contrasting family compatibility with a single creation hook.
closing.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → A factory encourages compatibility; it does not prove it

question.prompt: Give one sentence that distinguishes this chapter from Factory Method.
question.answer: Abstract Factory coordinates several related product roles through one selected family object; Factory Method varies a creation hook in an inherited workflow.
